337 {/* navigation links */} 338
339 ``` 340 341 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 342 ::view-transition-group(site-header) { 343 animation: none; 344 z-index: 100; 345 } 346 ::view-transition-old(site-header) { 347 display: none; 348 } 349 ::view-transition-new(site-header) { 350 animation: none; 351 } 352 ``` 353 354 The `display: none` on the old snapshot prevents a flash where both old and new headers are briefly visible. The pair together creates a handoff: the placeholder yields to the real thing. 149 150 Wrap the Suspense fallback in a `ViewTransition` with an exit animation, and the content in a `ViewTransition` with an enter animation: 151 152 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 153 import { Suspense, ViewTransition } from 'react' 154 155 export default async function PhotoPage({ params }) { 156 const { id } = await params 157 158 return ( 159 162 163 164 } 165 > 166 167 168 169 170 ) 171 } 172 ``` 173 174 As in Step 1, `default="none"` prevents this `ViewTransition` from animating during unrelated transitions, like the shared element morph. 175 176 The CSS animations use asymmetric timing. The exit is fast (150ms). The enter fade is slower (210ms) and delayed until the exit completes, while its slide movement runs longer (400ms): 177 178 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 179 :root { 180 --duration-exit: 150ms; 181 --duration-enter: 210ms; 182 --duration-move: 400ms; 183 } 184 185 ::view-transition-old(.slide-down) { 186 animation: 187 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both fade reverse, 188 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both slide-y reverse; 189 } 190 ::view-transition-new(.slide-up) { 191 animation: 192 var(--duration-enter) ease-in var(--duration-exit) both fade, 193 var(--duration-move) ease-in both slide-y; 194 } 195 196 @keyframes fade { 197 from { 198 filter: blur(3px); 199 opacity: 0; 200 } 201 to { 202 filter: blur(0); 203 opacity: 1; 204 } 205 } 206 @keyframes slide-y { 207 from { 208 transform: translateY(10px); 209 } 210 to { 211 transform: translateY(0); 212 } 213 } 214 ``` 215 216 The asymmetry is deliberate. Old content should leave quickly so it does not compete for attention. New content should arrive more gently so the user has time to register it. The `var(--duration-exit)` delay on the enter fade means the new content waits for the old content to finish leaving before it becomes visible. 217 218 If we refresh the page, the skeleton slides down and fades out, and a moment later the real content slides up and fades in. 219 220 ### Step 3: Add directional motion for navigation 221 222 The gallery now has morphing images and animated loading states. But navigating between pages still has no directional signal. Forward and back navigations look identical. The user cannot tell from the animation whether they moved deeper into the app or returned to a previous page. 223 224 In film and animation, horizontal direction encodes spatial position. Moving left means progressing forward (like turning a page in a left-to-right language). Moving right means going back. This convention is so ingrained that violating it feels disorienting. 225 226 Use the `transitionTypes` prop on `` to tag forward navigations: 227 228 ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 229 230 {/* photo thumbnail */} 231 232 ``` 233 234 The same pattern works for any navigation within the app. For example, previous/next arrows on a photo detail page can use `nav-back` and `nav-forward` to animate in the corresponding direction. 235 236 For links that return the user to a previous page, use `nav-back`: 237 238 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 239 240 ← Gallery 241 242 ``` 243 244 The transition type is not automatic. You decide which links are "forward" and which are "back" based on your app's navigation hierarchy. 245 246 Then wrap page content in a `ViewTransition` that maps transition types to directional animations: 247 248 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 249 262 {/* page content */} 263 264 ``` 265 266 The `enter` and `exit` props accept an object keyed by transition type. When a navigation carries the `nav-forward` type, the exit animation slides old content left and the enter animation slides new content in from the right. The `default: "none"` ensures that transitions without a type (browser back/forward, `router.refresh()`, Suspense reveals) produce no directional animation. 267 268 Wrap every participating page the same way. For the gallery to slide out on forward navigation and back in on `nav-back`, its page needs the same wrapper. Put the wrapper in each `page.tsx`, not the layout. Layouts persist across navigations, so enter and exit never fire there: 269 270 ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" 271 284 285 286 ``` 287 288 The CSS for directional slides: 289 290 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 291 ::view-transition-old(.nav-forward) { 292 --slide-offset: -60px; 293 animation: 294 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 295 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 296 } 297 ::view-transition-new(.nav-forward) { 298 --slide-offset: 60px; 299 animation: 300 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 301 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 302 } 303 304 ::view-transition-old(.nav-back) { 305 --slide-offset: 60px; 306 animation: 307 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 308 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 309 } 310 ::view-transition-new(.nav-back) { 311 --slide-offset: -60px; 312 animation: 313 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 314 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 315 } 316 317 @keyframes slide { 318 from { 319 translate: var(--slide-offset); 320 } 321 to { 322 translate: 0; 323 } 324 } 325 ``` 326 327 The 60px offset is enough to communicate direction without making the user track a fast-moving element across the screen. 328 329 #### Anchoring the header 330 331 During directional slides, the header should not move. A sliding header breaks the user's spatial anchor. They need one fixed reference point to understand that the _content_ moved, not the entire viewport. 332 333 Assign the header a `viewTransitionName` and suppress its animation in CSS: 334 335 ```tsx filename="components/header.tsx" 336
337 {/* navigation links */} 338
339 ``` 340 341 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 342 ::view-transition-group(site-header) { 343 animation: none; 344 z-index: 100; 345 } 346 ::view-transition-old(site-header) { 347 display: none; 348 } 349 ::view-transition-new(site-header) { 350 animation: none; 351 } 352 ``` 353 354 The `display: none` on the old snapshot prevents a flash where both old and new headers are briefly visible. The `z-index: 100` ensures the header renders above the sliding content. 355 356 If we navigate forward to a photo, content slides left. If we click the "← Gallery" link (tagged with `nav-back`), content slides right. The header stays fixed throughout both transitions. 357 358 Browser-initiated back navigations (the back button or swipe gestures) do not carry a transition type, so the directional slide does not play. The shared element morph from Step 1 still applies if both pages have matching `name` props. 359 360 #### Keeping the page interactive 361 362 While a transition runs, the `::view-transition` overlay captures pointer events, so clicks during the animation are lost. Let them pass through to the live page: 363 364 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 365 ::view-transition { 366 pointer-events: none; 367 } 368 ``` 369 370 This restores interactivity for unnamed content. Hit-testing still skips named participants (like the anchored header) for the transition's duration, so keep transitions short and avoid naming elements the user clicks rapidly. 371 372 #### Respecting reduced motion 373 374 Directional slides simulate physical movement across the viewport. This is the most common trigger for motion sensitivity. Morphs, reveals, and crossfades carry less risk since they affect smaller areas or rely on opacity rather than position. 375 376 The simplest approach is to disable all animation durations: 377 378 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 379 @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { 380 ::view-transition-old(*), 381 ::view-transition-new(*), 382 ::view-transition-group(*) { 383 animation-duration: 0s !important; 384 animation-delay: 0s !important; 385 } 386 } 387 ``` 388 389 Without animation, content swaps instantly, which is the browser's default behavior. A more refined approach would preserve crossfades and opacity transitions while removing positional movement. See ["No Motion Isn't Always prefers-reduced-motion"](https://css-tricks.com/nuking-motion-with-prefers-reduced-motion/) for more on this. 390 391 ### Step 4: Crossfade content within the same route 392 393 The gallery has a photographer section with tabs. Each tab shows a different photographer's photos, but the route structure is the same: `/collection/[slug]`. Clicking between tabs does not feel like navigating to a new page. It feels like switching content within the same container. 394 395 A directional slide would be wrong here. Slides communicate "going to a new place." A crossfade communicates "same place, different content." The container persists (continuity), only the grid inside changes (swap). 396 397 Use a `ViewTransition` with `key` set to the current slug. When the key changes, React triggers a transition between the old and new content: 398 399 ```tsx filename="app/collection/[slug]/page.tsx" 400 import { Suspense, ViewTransition } from 'react' 401 402 export default async function CollectionPage({ params }) { 403 const { slug } = await params 404 405 return ( 406 }> 407 414 415 416 417 ) 418 } 419 ``` 420 421 The `share="auto"` and `enter="auto"` props tell React to use its default crossfade animation. The `name` prop gives the container an identity so React knows what to animate. The navigation triggers the transition; the `key={slug}` change makes React treat the old and new content as an exit/enter pair (activating `share`) instead of an in-place update. 422 423 If we click between photographer tabs, the grid crossfades. The tab bar and surrounding layout do not move. Only the photo grid transitions between states. 424 425 ## Next steps 426 427 You now know how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation. Shared elements communicate continuity across routes. Suspense reveals animate loading handoffs. Directional slides encode navigation history. Crossfades signal content changes within the same location. 428 429 Each pattern answers a different question for the user: 430 431 | Pattern | What it communicates | 432 | ---------------------- | ------------------------------- | 433 | Shared element (morph) | "Same thing, going deeper" | 434 | Suspense reveal | "Data loaded" | 435 | Directional slide | "Going forward / coming back" | 436 | Same-route crossfade | "Same place, different content" | 437 438 For API details and more patterns: 439 440 - [Link `transitionTypes` prop](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#transitiontypes) 441 - [`useRouter`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-router), which also supports `transitionTypes` in `push()` and `replace()` 442 - [React `ViewTransition` component](https://react.dev/reference/react/ViewTransition) 443 - [Complete CSS from this guide](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo/blob/main/src/app/globals.css) — all keyframes and view transition rules in one file 444
